speaker_role: former Pomona College and Holy Cross admissions officer (Tom Campbell), via College Essay Guy channel
commercial_incentive: Ends with a pitch for the channel's paid one-on-one college counseling program.
key_insights: Recommends taking close to four full years each of English, math, science, social studies/history, and a foreign language, with increasing difficulty over time, as the baseline core academic pattern colleges like to see.

GPA and rigor are read together: a 3.7 earned via a consistently challenging (AP/honors) schedule often tells a stronger academic story to selective colleges than a 4.0 earned by avoiding advanced classes.
A B or higher in a harder class is usually a reasonable trade-off; patterns of C's or below in advanced classes are what actually concerns admissions readers, not an occasional B.
There's no fixed 'right number' of advanced classes per year; colleges reward sustainable consistency (e.g., 1-2 advanced classes done well every year) over overloading and burning out.

Admissions officers compare each applicant only against what was offered at their own high school, not against applicants nationally — some elite schools like Phillips Exeter offer no AP classes at all, and that's read via the school profile.
Electives matter less than core academic classes for rigor evaluation, but consistent low effort/checked-out behavior in electives is still noticed.

For competitive/impacted intended majors (engineering, CS, business, pre-med), colleges expect some relevant preparation (e.g., upper-level math/science); discovering the interest late is fine if the student takes visible steps to catch up, such as a summer community college course or independent research.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker's own institutional background: former admissions officer at Pomona College and Holy Cross.
Speaker explicitly frames >10% acceptance rate elite schools as 'highly rejective' when discussing tolerance for B grades in rigorous classes.
notable_or_distinctive: Names Phillips Exeter specifically as a top boarding school that offers zero AP classes, used to illustrate that rigor is judged relative to what a student's own school offers, not an absolute checklist.
reliability_notes: Fast-paced, short-form 'FAQ' video with generalized claims stated as near-universal admissions logic; ends in a sales pitch for the channel's paid counseling program, which may color the framing.
